Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette:
Daniel Tran was 35, a UX designer who had always prided himself on being calm, precise, and dependable. That sense of himself changed after a winter morning when a viral illness he had assumed would pass turned into a medical emergency. He had gone from shivering at home to struggling to breathe, watching his wife call an ambulance while he tried and failed to keep up with what the paramedics were saying. The fluorescent lights, the beeping monitors, the cold pressure of repeated physical examinations, and the long hours in the hospital settled into his memory as a single, unbearable stretch of fear. Even after he was discharged, he could not make the experience feel finished. He would replay the hospital corridor, the ambulance doors, and the sensation of his own body betraying him, but he now forced himself away from those thoughts almost immediately. He had come to believe there was something wrong with him as a person, that he was weak, and that he was no longer the steady man his family needed. At times he described feeling dead inside, as if the illness had taken something essential from him and left only a numb shell. Because of that, he steered clear of anything that might bring the event back into focus. He avoided hospitals and ambulances entirely, refused routine checkups, and found excuses to skip even minor physical examinations.

In the months that followed, Daniel’s sense that his body had failed him fed his fear that he was defective and fragile, and that belief made every sign of bodily strain feel dangerous. He began avoiding anything that put his body under stress: he stopped running, carried groceries in smaller loads, and made his schedule around not getting out of breath. He told himself that if exertion had once tipped him into crisis, then pushing himself again would be foolish. At work, where he sat in front of design mockups for most of the day, he became increasingly careful about anything that might leave him physically taxed. He would take the stairs only if he absolutely had to, and when colleagues suggested a lunchtime walk he often declined, saying he had too much to do. These choices offered short-term relief, but they also left his world shrinking around the fear that his body might fail again.

Daniel’s threat system stayed on a hair trigger. When a delivery arrived late, when his wife was delayed getting home, or when a meeting ran longer than expected, he assumed something bad was happening. He would check his phone repeatedly and feel his chest tighten until he had some explanation, and even then he found it impossible to trust reassurance for long. When his wife told him he was safe, or when his primary care office’s receptionist explained that the doctor was simply behind schedule, he could not really believe them. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react, as if it were waiting for the next sign of collapse. That state of alertness, in turn, made the medical world feel even more dangerous, and it strengthened his conviction that he should stay away from anything that might expose him to the possibility of being examined, delayed, or told that he was not actually safe. The more he watched for danger, the more he saw it everywhere, and the more convinced he became that he could not rely on anyone else’s word about his condition.

His avoidance gave the fear a life of its own. Each skipped appointment, each refusal to talk about what had happened, and each decision not to push his body seemed to confirm that the threat was real and still present. Because he would not think about the event for more than a moment, there was no chance to settle it in his mind; instead, the memory stayed raw and unfinished, returning most sharply when he was alone and his mind drifted toward his breathing or heartbeat. He began structuring his days around preventing that alarm from being activated, but the pattern only made him more vigilant. If a reply from a doctor’s office took too long, he assumed the worst. If his own body felt slightly off, he scanned it for signs of the same downward slide that had landed him in the ambulance. In that way, the fear he tried to avoid kept circling back, and his efforts to protect himself reinforced the very sense of danger he was trying to escape.

By the time he came to therapy, Daniel was exhausted by how much of his life had been organized around not being reminded of the illness. He had finally sought help after his wife noticed how often he refused appointments and how tense he remained even on ordinary days. What brought him in was not only the fear of becoming ill again, but the growing sense that he was losing confidence in his own body, his work, and his marriage. He hoped treatment might help him feel safe enough to stop living as though danger were always about to arrive, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he was, in fact, weak in the way he now believed.
